approachQuestion.prompt:
Badge tokens

n participants stand in a fixed line with integer ratings. Give each at least one token. Whenever adjacent participants have different ratings, the higher-rated participant must receive strictly more tokens than that neighbor. Equal ratings impose no comparison. Return the minimum total tokens.

Example 1: ratings=[1,3,2] → 4 with tokens [1,2,1].
Example 2: ratings=[3,2,1] → 6 with [3,2,1].
Example 3: ratings=[2,2] → 2.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 0 ≤ ratings[i] ≤ 10^9. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Allocate tokens initialized to one. Scan left to right, setting tokens[i]=tokens[i-1]+1 when rating[i]>rating[i-1]. Scan right to left; when rating[i]>rating[i+1], replace tokens[i] by max(tokens[i],tokens[i+1]+1). Sum the array.
options.feedback: The first scan gives the minimum required by each increasing run from the left. The reverse scan enforces the independent right-neighbor lower bound, taking a maximum to preserve the left constraint. Every assigned amount is forced by at least one of those bounds.

options.text: Use only the left-to-right scan and sum its tokens.
options.feedback: Descending runs require the opposite constraint. For [2,1], this gives [1,1], which violates the rule.

options.text: In the reverse scan, overwrite tokens[i] with tokens[i+1]+1 whenever rating[i]>rating[i+1], without taking a maximum.
options.feedback: An overwrite can break a longer increasing run. For [1,2,3,4,1], the first scan gives [1,2,3,4,1]; overwriting the peak with 2 violates its left neighbor.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

feedback.reason: The first scan gives the minimum required by each increasing run from the left. The reverse scan enforces the independent right-neighbor lower bound, taking a maximum to preserve the left constraint. Every assigned amount is forced by at least one of those bounds.

The forward pass satisfies increasing-rating requirements from the left. The backward pass adds right-neighbor requirements without lowering earlier allocations, using max. Equal ratings impose no strict token ordering.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above, including its auxiliary array. Allocate the array once and use iterative scans; do not copy the input. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

options.text: Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)

feedback.reason: Two directional passes and a sum use one n-entry token array.

messages.text: The specified method stores a linear array.
No scan restarts for each position.
There is no sorting or logarithmic search.

details: A constant number of linear scans takes O(n) time. The explicitly stored array has n entries and takes O(n) auxiliary space; there is no recursive stack.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(1)”: The specified method stores a linear array.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(n)”: No scan restarts for each position.
“Time O(n log n), auxiliary space O(n)”: There is no sorting or logarithmic search.
